questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish point from nonpoint sources of pollution
questions.stem: Clinic note 14: a household well beside a dairy shows nitrate rising after heavy rain, while a second well near a ploughed field is clean. What distinguishes the two sources of pollution?

options.text: The dairy is a point source with one discharge pipe; the field runoff is a nonpoint source.
Both are nonpoint sources, since rain washed contaminants into both wells.
options.misconception: treats a single pipe discharge as a diffuse source

options.text: Both are point sources, because each can be traced to one farm that owns it.
options.misconception: believes a single responsible farm makes a source point-like

options.text: Neither counts as pollution, since both contaminants originate in natural soil.
options.misconception: denies that farm-derived contaminants count as pollution

questions.explanation: A point source enters the environment through one identifiable discharge, while a nonpoint source arrives by many diffuse routes such as runoff from many fields. One farm can host both kinds of discharge, so ownership does not decide the classification.
questions.hint: Look for a single identifiable outlet.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the management differences between point and nonpoint sources
questions.stem: Clinic note 15: a public health nurse is asked why a single discharge pipe is regulated while runoff from many farms is not. Explain the difference in how the two source types are managed.

answer.exemplar: A point source has one measurable outlet, so its discharge can be sampled, permitted and monitored against a limit, and the responsible operator can be held to it. A nonpoint source arrives as diffuse runoff or leaching spread across a whole catchment, so no single outlet can be sampled and no single party owns the load. Managing it therefore relies on catchment-wide measures such as buffer strips, cover crops and limits on fertiliser or manure inputs, and on verifying the result by sampling the water body itself.

questions.explanation: Point sources can be controlled at the end of the pipe, whereas diffuse loads must be reduced across many decisions in the catchment. Sampling the receiving water is then the only way to check whether the catchment measures worked.
questions.hint: Control point sources at the pipe, diffuse ones across the catchment.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the combined thickness of named soil horizons
questions.stem: A soil profile dug for a clinic garden has a 5 cm litter layer, a 20 cm topsoil horizon and a 35 cm subsoil horizon above weathered parent material. What is the combined depth in centimetres from the surface to the top of the parent material?
questions.explanation: Adding the three layers gives 5 plus 20 plus 35, which is 60 centimetres. The litter layer counts as part of the profile from the surface even though it is not a mineral horizon in the strict sense.
questions.hint: Add the three thicknesses together.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a regulatory listing of criteria pollutants

stimulus.body: The district air quality notice lists six criteria pollutants for which ambient standards have been adopted, including ozone, particulate matter and lead. Monitoring stations report each of them on a published schedule so that results can be compared directly with the standard for that pollutant.

questions.stem: Clinic note 18: an air quality notice for the district lists ozone, particulate matter and lead as criteria pollutants on a published monitoring schedule. What does that listing tell a clinic considering an asthma campaign?

options.text: These are the three most dangerous pollutants in the district, ranked by harm to health.
options.misconception: reads a regulatory listing as a toxicity ranking

options.text: These pollutants have adopted standards, so measured levels can be compared with limits and acted upon.
These three come only from vehicles and factories, since other sources are exempt.
options.misconception: invents an exemption for other source types

options.text: These are pollutants that are safe at any level, so the clinic need not act on them.
options.misconception: confuses a monitored pollutant with a harmless one

questions.explanation: Being listed as a criteria pollutant means a standard exists, so a monitoring result can be judged against a limit. The listing says nothing about relative toxicity ranking and does not exempt any source type.
questions.hint: Standards exist, so measurements can be judged.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the condition under which groundwater counts as a renewable resource
questions.stem: Clinic note 22: a rural clinic is asked whether a district's groundwater supply counts as a renewable resource. Which statement about it is correct?

options.text: Groundwater is never renewable because recharge is always slower than demand.
options.misconception: treats all groundwater as non renewable whatever the recharge

options.text: Groundwater is always renewable because it is water that moves slowly through rock.
options.misconception: treats any groundwater as automatically renewable

options.text: Groundwater counts as renewable only while recharge keeps pace with the withdrawal.
Groundwater is renewable only when it is pumped for irrigation rather than drinking.
options.misconception: ties renewability to the type of use

questions.explanation: A resource is renewable only while it is replaced at least as fast as it is used, so recharge balance is the test for groundwater. Slow movement through rock says nothing about the balance, and the end use does not change it.
questions.hint: Compare recharge with withdrawal.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of each stage in a wastewater treatment train
questions.stem: Clinic note 24: a water quality officer explains a municipal treatment train to a visiting health team. Describe the stages in order and the purpose of each.

answer.exemplar: Screening comes first to remove rags, plastics and other debris that would damage pumps or clog later units. Primary settling then lets heavy solids and grease float or sink out in a calm tank, removing roughly half the suspended material. The biological stage adds air and microbes that oxidise dissolved and fine organic matter, which is where most of the biochemical oxygen demand goes. Finally disinfection is applied to inactivate remaining pathogens before discharge, once the load that could shield them has been removed.

questions.explanation: Each stage handles material of a different kind and size, from coarse debris down to dissolved organics and microbes. Sequencing matters because disinfection is only meaningful after the organic load that protects pathogens has been removed.
questions.hint: Coarse to fine, then solids, then microbes.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the chloride concentration after seawater mixes with a freshwater lens
questions.stem: Pumping into a coastal well draws 20 percent seawater at 35000 milligrams per litre into a freshwater lens holding 5000 milligrams per litre of chloride. What is the chloride concentration of the mixed well water in milligrams per litre?
questions.explanation: The mixture is a weighted average: 0.8 times 5000 gives 4000 and 0.2 times 35000 gives 7000, which sum to 11000 milligrams per litre. Mixing therefore pushes the concentration well above the drinking water guideline even though the lens itself was compliant.
questions.hint: Take a weighted average of the two concentrations.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a subsidence monitoring record

stimulus.body: Ground surface levels at three benchmarks in a pumping district have been surveyed each year since 2018. Over the five years of record the benchmarks have fallen 22 cm, 31 cm and 14 cm, and the district has increased its groundwater abstraction by roughly a fifth over the same period.

questions.stem: Clinic note 27: a monitoring record shows benchmarks in a pumping district falling 22 cm, 31 cm and 14 cm over five years while abstraction rose by a fifth. What does the record support?

options.text: The record shows rising land, because a lower benchmark reading means higher ground.
options.misconception: reads a fall in benchmark reading as a rise in the ground

options.text: The benchmarks have settled, because all three fell by a similar amount.
options.misconception: claims equal falls where the record shows unequal ones

options.text: The record proves the subsidence is caused only by pumping and nothing else.
options.misconception: treats correlation with abstraction as sole causation

options.text: Subsidence is occurring and is variable across the district, consistent with pumping-driven compaction.

questions.explanation: All three benchmarks fell, so the ground is sinking, and the unequal amounts show the subsidence varies across the district. The concurrent rise in abstraction is consistent with compaction, though a single record cannot prove that pumping is the only cause.
questions.hint: Falling benchmarks mean sinking ground.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Choose a sampling strategy suited to a nonpoint source
questions.stem: Clinic note 31: a public health nurse explains how her team traced an unexplained nitrate rise to diffuse farm runoff. Which sampling strategy is suited to that task?

options.text: Sample only the lowest point in the catchment, since all pollution flows downhill.
options.misconception: believes one low point represents a diffuse source

options.text: Sample many locations across the catchment, because diffuse sources vary from place to place.
Wait for one very large storm, since the largest event carries all the pollution.
options.misconception: assumes a single storm carries the whole diffuse load

options.text: Sample only farms with a known spill history, since diffuse sources begin with spills.
options.misconception: reduces a diffuse source to isolated spill events

questions.explanation: A diffuse source has no single entry point, so its contribution varies across the catchment and must be sampled over many locations. A single low point, a single storm or a list of known spills would all miss much of the load.
questions.hint: Diffuse sources need wide spatial sampling.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how soil horizon properties affect contaminant movement
questions.stem: Clinic note 33: a nurse asks why nitrate from a garden bed reaches the well below it while phosphorus does not. Explain the role of soil horizons in this difference.

answer.exemplar: The topsoil horizon is the part of the profile with most organic matter and biological activity, so nitrate produced by decomposition is held only weakly and moves readily downward in percolating water. Phosphorus, by contrast, binds strongly to iron and aluminium oxides and to organic matter, so in most soils it stays in the upper horizons and is taken up by plants. The subsoil and weathered parent material below have fewer binding sites, so anything that does pass the topsoil travels with the percolate toward the aquifer, which is why a shallow well is more exposed than a deep one.

questions.explanation: Nitrate is highly mobile because it is not held on soil particles, while phosphate is strongly adsorbed to iron, aluminium oxides and organic matter. The upper horizons therefore filter phosphorus while letting nitrate pass to the water table.
questions.hint: Nitrate is mobile, phosphate is strongly adsorbed.

questions.stem: An air monitoring station reports 30 micrograms per cubic metre of a pollutant whose primary standard is 75 micrograms per cubic metre. What percentage of the standard does the measured concentration reach?
questions.explanation: Dividing 30 by 75 gives 0.4, so the measured concentration is 40 percent of the standard. Expressing results this way allows readings for different pollutants to be compared against their own limits.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether a resource use is sustainable against its replenishment

stimulus.body: A forestry note records that the district harvested 9000 cubic metres of timber last year while the managed forest regrew 5000 cubic metres over the same period. The note adds that the district has met its replanting obligations in every year of the programme.

questions.stem: Clinic note 36: a forestry note records a harvest of 9000 cubic metres against regrowth of 5000 cubic metres. What does the note tell the clinic about long term wood supply?

options.text: Meeting replanting obligations means no timber is being removed from the forest.
options.misconception: treats replanting duties as proof of zero harvest

options.text: Harvest and regrowth balance each other, so the resource is being used sustainably.
options.misconception: mistakes total harvest for annual harvest when comparing

options.text: Harvest is running well ahead of regrowth, so the standing resource is being drawn down.
Regrowth of 5000 cubic metres means the forest holds at least that much timber today.
options.misconception: reads an annual regrowth figure as total standing stock

questions.explanation: Removing 9000 cubic metres while only 5000 are replaced draws the standing resource down by 4000 cubic metres each year. Meeting replanting duties shows the forest is being restocked, but it does not balance the harvest.
questions.hint: Compare what is removed with what is replaced.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Justify placing disinfection last in a treatment train
questions.stem: Clinic note 38: an inspector asks a plant operator why disinfection is the last stage of the treatment train. Which statement gives the correct reason?

options.text: Disinfection comes last because it is the weakest stage in the whole train.
options.misconception: calls disinfection the least effective stage

options.text: Disinfection comes last because it needs the longest contact time in the water.
options.misconception: explains sequencing by reaction time rather than purpose

options.text: Disinfection comes last because earlier stages would destroy the organisms it needs.
options.misconception: invents a dependence on microbes from earlier stages

options.text: Disinfection destroys the remaining pathogens once the load that shielded them is gone.

questions.explanation: Disinfection inactivates pathogens, which works best once solids and organic matter that could shelter them have been removed. Ordering it after the biological stage also avoids wasting chlorine on a heavy organic load.
questions.hint: Disinfection protects against what is left.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how pumping causes saltwater intrusion in coastal aquifers
questions.stem: Clinic note 40: a coastal health team is told that wells near the shore have become saline. Explain the mechanism that connects pumping to saltwater intrusion.

answer.exemplar: In a coastal aquifer a body of fresh water rests on denser seawater, and the interface between them slopes inland in what is known as the Ghyben Herzberg relation. Pumping lowers the hydraulic head of the fresh water, which reduces the pressure holding the interface offshore, so seawater moves inland and upward toward the pumping well. Chloride in the pumped water therefore rises even though nothing has been added to the aquifer, and the change becomes permanent if the cone of depression is allowed to reach the interface, because recovery of head then takes far longer than the damage.

questions.explanation: Pumping lowers the freshwater head, so the denser seawater is no longer held back and moves inland toward the well. The rising chloride is therefore a physical consequence of the head decline rather than a new contamination event.
questions.hint: Lower the freshwater head and the salt moves in.

questions.learningObjective: Compare subsidence rates between two monitored areas
questions.stem: In one block of a pumping district the ground fell 12 centimetres over 5 years, while in the neighbouring block it fell 9 centimetres over 3 years. How much faster, in centimetres per year, is the second block subsiding?
questions.explanation: The first block sank at 12 over 5, which is 2.4 centimetres per year, and the second at 9 over 3, which is 3.0 centimetres per year. The difference is 0.6 centimetres per year, so the second block is subsiding faster.
questions.hint: Convert each block to a rate, then subtract.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Apply a source classification to a real contamination case

stimulus.body: Water samples from a neighbourhood well show rising nitrate over two years, with the increase following the periods of heaviest rainfall. Upstream, a disused landfill and about forty hectares of recently ploughed land lie within the contributing catchment, and no single pipe discharge has been found discharging to the well.

questions.stem: Clinic note 42: an intake note records rising nitrate in a neighbourhood well, tracking heavy rainfall, with a disused landfill and forty hectares of ploughed land in the contributing catchment and no pipe discharge to the well. How should the clinic characterise the source?

options.text: A point source, because the disused landfill can be pinpointed on the catchment map.
options.misconception: treats any mapped site as a point source

options.text: Predominantly a nonpoint source, since the load tracks rainfall and no single discharge exists.
Neither type, because nitrate in groundwater is always a natural phenomenon.
options.misconception: denies that nitrate in groundwater can be contamination

options.text: A point source, because one well with a measurable concentration is a single outlet.
options.misconception: mistakes a monitoring point for a discharge point

questions.explanation: A load that rises and falls with rainfall and cannot be traced to one discharge indicates diffuse transport from the catchment. The landfill is one contributing area among many, and a monitoring well is not a source of pollution.
questions.hint: Rainfall response plus no single outlet means diffuse.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the soil layer that controls nitrate leaching to groundwater
questions.stem: Clinic note 45: a nurse explains to a farming family why nitrate applied after fertilising reaches their shallow well. Which soil layer matters most in that explanation?

options.text: The aquifer itself, which filters nutrients out before the water reaches the well.
options.misconception: assumes the aquifer removes nitrate from infiltrating water

options.text: The deep parent material, since nutrients travel through it fastest of all.
options.misconception: assigns rapid nutrient transport to the least reactive layer

options.text: The topsoil, where nitrates are weakly held and leach readily toward the aquifer.
The bedrock layer, where dissolved ions are held tightly on mineral surfaces.
options.misconception: assumes strong ion retention in bedrock

questions.explanation: Nitrate is not held on soil particles, so it moves down with percolating water out of the topsoil and into the saturated zone below. Adsorption of other ions onto iron and aluminium oxides is what slows some contaminants, and that is weak in the topsoil.
questions.hint: Nitrate is not retained on soil particles.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why criteria pollutants are regulated
questions.stem: Clinic note 47: a clinician is asked why some air pollutants receive formal standards while others do not. Explain how criteria pollutants are identified and what the standards are for.

answer.exemplar: A pollutant becomes a criteria pollutant when it has been recognised through scientific evidence as harmful to health at concentrations found in the ambient air, and when that evidence is strong enough to justify a numeric standard that can be met by control measures. The standard is a legal benchmark, not a statement about relative danger: each pollutant has its own limit and its own averaging period, set so that meeting it protects the most sensitive groups in the population. Monitoring against these limits lets regulators act and lets clinicians interpret risk in their community.

questions.explanation: Criteria pollutants are named because the evidence supports a legally enforceable limit, not because they are ranked by toxicity. Each pollutant has its own standard and averaging period, which makes measured results interpretable against the limit.
questions.hint: Standards follow the evidence and are legally enforceable.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the net annual drawdown of a renewable resource
questions.stem: A managed forest supplied 9000 cubic metres of timber to a district last year and regrew 5000 cubic metres over the same period. What was the net drawdown of the standing resource in cubic metres?
questions.explanation: Net drawdown is the harvest minus the regrowth, so 9000 minus 5000 gives 4000 cubic metres removed from the standing resource in that year. A continuing drawdown at this rate reduces the stock available for future harvest.
questions.hint: Subtract the regrowth from the harvest.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a monitoring result after a change in treatment performance

stimulus.body: Effluent biochemical oxygen demand from a treatment plant has risen from 20 to 55 milligrams per litre over six months. Rainfall records show three unusually heavy storms in that period, the plant has the same operators and the same chemical dosing schedule throughout, and the incoming wastewater flow rate rose by roughly forty percent during the storm months.

questions.stem: Clinic note 50: a plant note records effluent biochemical oxygen demand rising from 20 to 55 milligrams per litre over six months, with three heavy storms, unchanged staff and dosing, and influent flow up about forty percent. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The microbiological stage has improved, so the organic load reaching the water has grown.
options.misconception: claims improvement explains a rise in effluent load

options.text: The operators have dosed the chemicals incorrectly since the start of the period.
options.misconception: blames operator error despite an unchanged dosing schedule

options.text: The effluent standard has been relaxed, so the measured value has risen by definition.
options.misconception: mistakes a changed measurement for a changed standard

options.text: Storm inflows overwhelmed the plant capacity, so organic matter passed through untreated.

questions.explanation: The rise coincides with heavy storms and a forty percent higher flow, while the plant and its dosing are unchanged, which points to hydraulic overload in the biological stage. Storm inflows carry a high organic load and short retention time, so more organic matter passes through.
questions.hint: The timing matches the storm inflows, not the plant staff.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the mechanism by which pumping drives saltwater intrusion
questions.stem: Clinic note 52: a coastal practice reports that patients' well water became salty after a period of heavy pumping. Which mechanism best explains the change?

options.text: Pumping raises the water table and compresses the freshwater lens downward.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the water table change

options.text: Pumping lowers the water table and draws saltwater sideways into the well.
Salt enters because the well casing corrodes in contact with air above the lens.
options.misconception: blames casing corrosion for a hydrological process

options.text: Salt enters because drought alone concentrates salts without any pumping.
options.misconception: explains intrusion without the pumping trigger

questions.explanation: Drawing water down lowers the freshwater head, so the denser seawater is no longer held back offshore and moves inland toward the well. The result is a rise in chloride in the pumped water with no new contaminant added to the aquifer.
questions.hint: Lower the head and the salt moves inland.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how groundwater withdrawal causes the ground surface to sink
questions.stem: Clinic note 54: a district asks why the land over a pumped aquifer keeps sinking. Explain the mechanism and note which part of the process can be reversed.

answer.exemplar: Water in the pore spaces of an aquifer supports the grains of sediment and carries part of the load of the overlying ground. Pumping removes that water, so pore pressure falls and the weight previously carried by the water is transferred to the grain framework. Fine grained sediments, especially clays, then compact irreversibly as their particles are squeezed into a tighter arrangement, and the ground surface drops with them. Some of the subsidence is elastic and reverses when pumping stops and pressure recovers, but the compaction component does not, so long term land surface loss is permanent even when abstraction is reduced.

questions.explanation: Falling pore pressure transfers the load to the sediment framework, causing compaction of the aquifer and sinking of the surface above it. The elastic part of the subsidence can recover, but compaction of fine sediments cannot.
questions.hint: Loss of support water compacts the sediments.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a monitoring design for a diffuse pollution source

stimulus.body: A district proposes to judge its fertiliser reduction programme by sampling one large water quality station on the main river once each year, in late summer, and comparing the result with the same station in earlier years. No other stations are funded, and no flow data are collected at the time of sampling.

questions.stem: Clinic note 56: a district proposes judging its fertiliser programme with one annual sample from a single river station in late summer and no flow data. Which assessment of the proposal is correct?

options.text: It is sound, because late summer sampling avoids the dilution that spring floods produce.
options.misconception: treats a low flow season as a valid substitute for an annual load

options.text: It is sound, because a single fixed station gives a consistent long term record for comparison.
options.misconception: values consistency of location more than representativeness of the load

options.text: It is weak, because a single late summer sample can neither represent the catchment nor separate a load from flow.
It is weak only because the station should be moved to a smaller stream rather than the main river.
options.misconception: prescribes a different single station instead of broader sampling

questions.stem: Clinic note 59: a clinic's air quality file lists ozone, lead and nitrogen dioxide as criteria pollutants for a health campaign. Which statement best explains the role of that group?

options.text: They are pollutants shown to have no effect on health, so no action is needed.
options.misconception: confuses a monitored pollutant with a harmless one

options.text: They are the pollutants a clinic always measures first during a health emergency.
options.misconception: defines the group by clinical priority rather than regulation

options.misconception: restricts criteria pollutants to urban locations

options.text: They are named pollutants with adopted standards, so readings can be judged and acted upon.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how renewable resources are assessed for sustainable use
questions.stem: Clinic note 61: a public health officer is asked how a district should judge whether its water use is sustainable. Explain the test that should be applied to a renewable resource.

answer.exemplar: The test is whether the rate of replenishment keeps pace with the rate of withdrawal, assessed over a long enough period to include a full cycle of wet and dry years. For groundwater this means comparing pumping with recharge to the aquifer, and for forests or fisheries comparing harvest with regeneration or recruitment; where the resource also supports other uses, those demands have to be counted as well. A surplus may be stored for a bad year, but a persistent deficit is a drawdown of the stock, which converts a renewable resource into a slowly exhausted one and eventually into a non renewable supply.

questions.explanation: Renewability is a question of rates, not of labels, so replenishment must be compared with use over a full cycle. A persistent deficit draws down the stock and effectively converts the resource into a non renewable one.
questions.hint: Compare replenishment rate with withdrawal rate.

questions.learningObjective: Assess a well-siting proposal in a coastal aquifer

stimulus.body: A coastal water authority proposes replacing two failing wells with a single new well 150 metres from the shoreline, drawing 40 percent more water than the wells it replaces. questions.stem: Clinic note 64: an engineering proposal replaces two wells with one 150 metres from the shore, drawing forty percent more water, where the freshwater lens is thickest 900 metres inland. What should the clinic advise?

options.text: The siting reduces risk, since consolidating wells into one lowers total abstraction.
options.misconception: confuses consolidation with a reduction in volume pumped

options.text: The siting increases intrusion risk, since the well is close to the saline boundary and draws more.
The siting is acceptable, because the retreating shoreline boundary proves the lens is advancing.
options.misconception: reverses what a retreating saline boundary indicates

options.text: The siting is acceptable, because well depth rather than distance controls intrusion risk.
options.misconception: claims depth alone governs the risk of intrusion

questions.explanation: The saline boundary has already retreated inland, so a well only 150 metres from the shore sits close to it, and drawing forty percent more water would pull the interface further inland. Siting nearer the thick inland part of the lens and managing the pumping rate would reduce the risk.
questions.hint: The boundary has moved inland, and pumping increases.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the cause of subsidence above a pumped aquifer
questions.stem: Clinic note 67: a district asks why the land surface over a pumped aquifer keeps sinking. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The land sinks because heat from the pumps expands the rock beneath the town.
options.misconception: invents thermal expansion of rock caused by pumping

options.text: The land sinks because the soil above it is washed away by river erosion.
options.misconception: blames surface erosion for a subsurface compaction process

options.text: Groundwater removal lowers pore pressure, so the compacting aquifer sinks with the surface.
The land sinks because buildings add weight to the ground surface.
options.misconception: attributes subsidence to structural load alone

questions.explanation: Removing groundwater lowers pore pressure, transferring load to the sediment grains, which compact and drag the ground surface down with them. Erosion acts at the surface and heat from pumps does not expand rock, so neither explains a sinking ground over an aquifer.
questions.hint: Think about what the water was holding up.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a catchment must be managed as a whole for diffuse loads
questions.stem: Clinic note 69: a nurse is asked how a district should reduce the nitrate that reaches its wells from farming. Explain why the response must work across the catchment.

answer.exemplar: Because the load arrives at the well from many fields rather than from one outlet, no single action can remove it, and the actions of neighbouring farms combine on the same aquifer. A buffer strip along a watercourse, cover crops over the winter, reduced application rates of nitrogen fertiliser, and restrictions on when manure may be spread all act on the pathway of the water itself, so the benefit of one measure depends on what the neighbours do. The only way to know whether the programme is working is to sample the groundwater across the catchment and in the streams that feed it, and to compare those results with the same monitoring from before the scheme began.

questions.explanation: Diffuse loads are the sum of many small decisions across the catchment, so they need many coordinated measures applied together. Catchment-wide monitoring is what confirms whether those combined measures are working.
questions.hint: The load is the sum of many decisions.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a total nonpoint pollutant load across a catchment
questions.stem: A catchment of 500 hectares loses 20 kilograms of phosphorus per hectare each year from fertiliser runoff. What is the total phosphorus load carried to the river in kilograms per year?
questions.explanation: The load is the area multiplied by the loss rate, so 500 hectares times 20 kilograms per hectare gives 10000 kilograms per year. Because the loss rate is per hectare, this calculation is the standard way to total a diffuse load.
questions.hint: Multiply the area by the loss per hectare.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a soil profile described in a field record

stimulus.body: A soil pit described from the surface downward shows a dark crumbly layer rich in roots and organic matter 25 centimetres thick, a paler sandy layer beneath it 60 centimetres thick with few roots, and weathered rock fragments below that. The pale layer becomes strongly mottled with red and grey patches at 1.5 metres depth.

questions.stem: Clinic note 72: a field description records a dark rooty layer 25 centimetres thick, a pale sandy layer 60 centimetres thick, and strong red and grey mottling at 1.5 metres. What does the mottling indicate?

options.text: Excellent aeration, since the mottled colours show air reaching this depth.
options.misconception: reads red and grey mottling as evidence of aeration

options.text: The start of the parent material, so the weathered rock layer has been reached.
options.misconception: reads colour mottling as a change of parent material

options.text: Heavy contamination by iron ore dust deposited on the soil surface.
options.misconception: treats red grey mottling as surface contamination

options.text: Periodic saturation and reduction, so water is standing in the lower horizon for part of the year.

questions.explanation: Red and grey mottling together are the classic sign of alternating wetting and drying in a waterlogged zone, where iron is reduced to grey when saturated and re-oxidised to red when drained. This marks a perched water table and points to poor drainage rather than good aeration.
questions.hint: Red and grey mottles mean wet and dry cycles.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why point sources are easier to regulate than diffuse sources
questions.stem: Clinic note 75: a nurse asks why regulating a single discharge pipe is easier than regulating runoff from a whole catchment. Which reason is correct?

options.text: Runoff carries far less pollutant mass than any single discharge pipe.
options.misconception: claims diffuse sources carry a negligible load

options.text: A single outfall can be measured and permitted directly; diffuse runoff cannot.
Discharge pipes are easier to regulate because they are usually on private land.
options.misconception: ties ease of regulation to land ownership

options.text: Runoff is regulated only after it reaches the river, so it can never be intercepted.
options.misconception: claims runoff can never be intercepted upstream

questions.explanation: A point source has one outlet whose discharge can be sampled, permitted and monitored against a limit, with a named operator responsible. Diffuse runoff has no such outlet or owner, so it has to be managed through catchment-wide measures and verified in the receiving water.
questions.hint: One outlet means one measurable permit.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Justify the order of operations in a treatment train
questions.stem: Clinic note 77: an operator asks why the order of a treatment train cannot be rearranged. Explain what would go wrong if the stages were swapped.

answer.exemplar: The order follows the size and character of the material to be removed. Solids screening must precede pumping, because rags and plastics would foul the pumps and clog the aeration diffusers, and primary settling must precede the biological stage, because the heavy grit and grease it removes would otherwise smother the microbial floc and consume the oxygen supply. Aeration must precede disinfection, since a chlorine dose applied to raw wastewater is largely consumed by the organic load it is meant to inactivate pathogens in. Disinfection must be last, because any stage after it would reintroduce organisms into water that has already been treated.

questions.explanation: Each stage depends on the one before it: screens protect the pumps, settling protects the microbes, aeration removes the load that would consume chlorine. Reversing the order wastes chemicals, damages equipment and leaves pathogens untreated.
questions.hint: Each stage protects and enables the next.

questions.learningObjective: Project chloride levels from a known rate of increase
questions.stem: A coastal well's chloride level starts at 120 milligrams per litre and rises by 8 milligrams per litre for each week of heavy pumping. What will the level be after 12 weeks of pumping?
questions.explanation: Twelve weeks of pumping adds 12 times 8, which is 96 milligrams per litre, to the starting 120. The result of 216 milligrams per litre is well above a typical drinking water guideline, which is why pumping is curtailed.
questions.hint: Multiply weeks by the weekly rise and add the start.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a subsidence record with a partial recovery

stimulus.body: Benchmark levels in a coastal district show the ground fell 40 centimetres between 1998 and 2010 while groundwater abstraction peaked. Abstraction was reduced by half from 2011, and the benchmarks have since risen by 3 centimetres, so the ground now sits 37 centimetres below its 1998 level.

questions.stem: Clinic note 79: a record shows the ground fell 40 centimetres while abstraction peaked, then rose 3 centimetres after abstraction was halved. How should the clinic interpret this recovery?

options.text: No recovery, because a falling ground level can never rise again.
options.misconception: denies that elastic rebound is possible at all

options.text: Full recovery, because the benchmarks have risen since abstraction was reduced.
options.misconception: treats a small rebound as complete recovery of the surface

options.text: Partly elastic recovery, but the ground remains far below its original level because compaction is lasting.
Continued subsidence, because the benchmarks rose by only 3 centimetres in total.
options.misconception: reads a small rise as evidence of continuing sinking

questions.explanation: The 3 centimetre rebound is the elastic component returning as pore pressure recovers, while the remaining 37 centimetres is permanent compaction of the aquifer. Because the two components behave differently, reducing pumping slows the sinking but does not undo it.
questions.hint: Some of the sinking is elastic and some is permanent.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Choose a management split for mixed point and nonpoint sources
questions.stem: Clinic note 81: a clinic reviews a catchment where one large plant and many small farms contribute the same pollutant. Which management approach fits the sources involved?

options.text: Regulate neither, since a catchment with two source types is automatically clean.
options.misconception: treats source diversity as evidence of cleanliness

options.text: Regulate only the plant, since its contribution is easier to measure.
options.misconception: ignores the diffuse load because it is harder to measure

options.text: Regulate only the farms, since the plant output is diluted by the river flow.
options.misconception: excuses the point source because of river dilution

options.text: Regulate the plant at its outfall and address the farms through catchment-wide measures.

questions.explanation: Each source type needs the instrument that fits it: the plant through a permit at its discharge, the farms through measures applied across the catchment. Leaving either one out simply shifts the load to whichever part is not regulated.
questions.hint: Match the instrument to each type of source.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a diffuse pollution source is identified from monitoring data
questions.stem: Clinic note 83: a health team must decide whether a rising nitrate concentration in a well comes from a single discharge or from diffuse land use. Explain how the two would be distinguished using monitoring evidence.

answer.exemplar: A point source produces a signal with a fixed relationship to its discharge: the concentration rises and falls with the flow from that outfall, the source can be located by upstream sampling, and the load stays proportional to the discharge even as dilution changes. Diffuse land use instead produces concentrations that track rainfall and seasonal fertiliser applications, vary from sampling point to point across the catchment, and show no single upstream location that explains them. Comparing head gradient and flow records with the concentration record separates the two, since a point source can be matched to a known discharge while a diffuse load is only accounted for by summing the catchment.

questions.explanation: The signatures differ in time, in space and in their response to flow, so rainfall response and spatial variation identify a diffuse source. Only a diffuse source shows up as the summed contribution of many small inputs.
questions.hint: Compare timing, spatial pattern and flow response.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the mass of organic matter held in a topsoil layer
questions.stem: A topsoil horizon 10 centimetres thick has a bulk density of 1.3 grams per cubic centimetre and contains 3 percent organic matter by mass. What mass of organic matter does one square metre of that layer hold, in kilograms?
questions.explanation: One square metre over 10 centimetres holds 100000 cubic centimetres, which at 1.3 grams per cubic centimetre is 130000 grams or 130 kilograms of soil. Three percent of that is 3.9 kilograms of organic matter per square metre, the stock that sustains soil structure and water holding capacity.
questions.hint: Find the soil mass first, then take the percentage.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret how a criterion pollutant standard is used in monitoring

stimulus.body: A monitoring bulletin reports a rolling average concentration for a criteria pollutant together with the standard that applies to it and the averaging period over which the standard is defined. Where the rolling average exceeds the standard, the bulletin notes that exceedances are counted for regulatory purposes and advises sensitive groups to reduce outdoor activity.

questions.stem: Clinic note 86: a bulletin pairs each rolling average with its standard and averaging period, and advises sensitive groups to limit outdoor activity during exceedances. How should the clinic use this bulletin?

options.text: Treat any single high reading as an exceedance, since the rolling average only smooths the data.
options.misconception: ignores the averaging period that defines the standard

options.text: Compare each rolling average with the standard for the same averaging period before advising patients.
Ignore exceedances, since a rolling average always understates the true concentration.
options.misconception: asserts that averaging always reduces measured values

options.text: Use the bulletin only for research, since it carries no regulatory status.
options.misconception: denies the regulatory role stated in the bulletin

questions.explanation: A standard is defined for a specific averaging period, so a rolling average is only comparable with the standard that uses the same period. Comparing a single reading against a standard built for a different averaging basis would produce false exceedances or missed ones.
questions.hint: Match the averaging period to the standard.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the upgrade that improves a failing biological stage
questions.stem: Clinic note 88: a town's treatment train fails after storms, with effluent biochemical oxygen demand rising sharply during high flows. Which change would most improve the biological stage?

options.text: Raise the disinfectant dose, since a low dose is why the biology fails.
options.misconception: blames the disinfection stage for biological failure

options.text: Add more screens, since debris is the main cause of biological stage failure.
options.misconception: attributes biological failure mainly to screen debris

options.text: Add capacity for the extra flow, so the organisms are not washed out of the reactor.
Warm the effluent, since bacteria cannot work in cold water.
options.misconception: offers a temperature fix for a hydraulic cause

questions.explanation: The pattern of failure at high flow points to hydraulic overload, where the retention time in the biological reactor is too short for the organisms to process the organic load. Extra reactor capacity fixes that, while screens, disinfectant dose and temperature do not address the cause.
questions.hint: Failures that track storm flow need more capacity.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a coastal water authority can reduce the risk of intrusion
questions.stem: Clinic note 90: a coastal water authority asks the clinic for advice on keeping its wells within the freshwater lens. Describe the measures that reduce the risk of saltwater intrusion.

answer.exemplar: The measures act on the cone of depression, which is the drop in hydraulic head that forms around a pumping well and allows seawater to move inland. Abstraction can be spread across more wells and more hours, since the same volume drawn in a flatter pattern creates a shallower cone, and pumping can be reduced when the shoreline boundary is already close. Converting the most productive coastal wells to fresh water storage and recharge basins reduces the pressure on the lens while also building a buffer. Management is further supported by continuous monitoring of chloride and of the position of the interface, so that the rate of retreat can be compared with the rate of abstraction and adjusted before salinity reaches the patients.

questions.explanation: Every measure reduces the height of the cone of depression or slows the retreat of the saline boundary. Distributed pumping and recharge keep the head higher, and monitoring shows whether abstraction is still outrunning the boundary.
questions.hint: Flatten the cone of depression and watch the boundary.

questions.stem: The ground surface in one district has sunk 45 centimetres over 30 years of monitored groundwater abstraction. What is the average rate of subsidence in centimetres per year?
questions.explanation: Dividing the total fall of 45 centimetres by the 30 years gives 1.5 centimetres per year. At that rate the ground loses a further 15 centimetres over a decade, which is enough to change the height of a surface water intake.
questions.hint: Divide the total fall by the number of years.

questions.learningObjective: Assess a mixed source catchment record

stimulus.body: A catchment note records a licensed discharge of 40 kilograms per day of phosphorus from a treatment works outlet, together with field surveys estimating 160 kilograms per day of phosphorus reaching the river from farmland across the catchment. The note adds that the river concentration at the downstream station has not changed over five years of monitoring.

questions.stem: Clinic note 94: a catchment note records 40 kilograms per day from a licensed outlet and 160 kilograms per day from farmland, with no change in downstream concentration. What does the record suggest?

options.text: The river is unaffected, because phosphorus from farmland never reaches flowing water.
options.misconception: claims a diffuse phosphorus load cannot reach the river

options.text: Most of the load is diffuse, so the licensed outlet can safely be ignored.
options.misconception: dismisses the point source once it is the smaller contributor

options.text: The concentration must be falling, since both sources add phosphorus to the same river.
options.misconception: assumes adding load always lowers a measured concentration

options.text: Most of the load is diffuse, and the steady concentration suggests the two sources together are near the limit.

questions.explanation: Four fifths of the estimated load comes from farmland, so the point source is the smaller part of the problem and the larger part needs catchment measures. A steady concentration with a steady total load suggests the river is near the level at which the load is being matched or diluted.
questions.hint: Compare the two loads and then the observed concentration.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why topsoil erodes more readily than subsoil
questions.stem: Clinic note 96: a gardener asks why topsoil washes away more easily than subsoil on a slope. Which statement explains the difference?

options.text: Subsoil is denser because it holds more weathered rock fragments than topsoil.
options.misconception: explains erosion resistance by rock fragments rather than binding agents

options.text: Topsoil has less clay and organic matter, so fewer particles bind the soil against erosion.
Topsoil is always at the top of the slope, so it is the first surface to be disturbed.
options.misconception: confuses position on the slope with erodibility

options.text: Subsoil resists erosion because it stays permanently frozen at depth.
options.misconception: invents permanent frost in the subsoil

questions.explanation: Clay and organic matter act as binding agents that hold soil particles together, and the topsoil has the least of them once organic residues have decomposed. Subsoil enriched in clay and iron oxides therefore resists erosion, which is why gullies typically cut into the subsoil last.
questions.hint: Binding agents decide how easily soil is moved.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how criteria pollutants fit into environmental health assessment
questions.stem: Clinic note 98: a respiratory clinic prepares a community air quality briefing. Explain how criteria pollutants should be used in that briefing.

answer.exemplar: The clinic should present each criteria pollutant against its own standard and averaging period, so that a measured value has a clear meaning: below the standard is the intended condition of the community, above it is an exceedance with a legal and public health significance. Because the standards are set to protect the most sensitive members of the population, an exceedance is a reason to advise that group specifically rather than to reassure the general public. The briefing should also distinguish a single exceedance from a persistent pattern, since it is the frequency and duration of exceedances that carries most of the health signal, and should state clearly where the monitoring station sits relative to the neighbourhoods being served.

questions.explanation: Each pollutant is only interpretable against its own standard and averaging period, and exceedances matter most for the most sensitive groups. Frequency and duration of exceedance carry more health meaning than a single reading.
questions.hint: Read every value against its own standard.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the volume of renewable supply that must replace a demand
questions.stem: A district's water demand is 24000 cubic metres per month, and rainfall recharge to the aquifer supplies 15000 cubic metres of that total each month. What volume must be withdrawn from a renewable aquifer each month to meet the demand?
questions.explanation: The demand of 24000 cubic metres minus the 15000 cubic metres of recharge leaves 9000 cubic metres to be met from another renewable source each month. If that volume is not replaced, the aquifer stock is being drawn down and the supply is no longer fully renewable.
questions.hint: Subtract the recharge from the total demand.

questions.learningObjective: Assess a monitoring record showing a treatment process going wrong

stimulus.body: A plant note records that the settled sludge blanket in the primary clarifier has risen steadily and is now being carried over into the aeration basin. The flow meter shows the same daily volume as last year, the incoming wastewater has the same character, and the chemical dosing has been checked and found unchanged.

questions.stem: Clinic note 100: a plant note reports a rising sludge blanket in the clarifier spilling into the aeration basin, with unchanged flow, waste character and dosing. What does the record indicate?

options.text: The inflow must have changed character, because the sludge blanket proves the waste is different.
options.misconception: ignores the note that the waste character is unchanged

options.text: The aeration basin is failing, because the sludge blanket is caused by insufficient aeration.
options.misconception: attributes a clarifier problem to the stage downstream

options.text: Solids are accumulating faster than they can settle, so the clarifier is overloaded or poorly operated.
Chemical dosing must have been mis-set, because no change in dosing would cause this pattern.
options.misconception: blames dosing the note records as unchanged

questions.explanation: A rising sludge blanket means solids are entering the clarifier faster than they can settle, and carryover into the aeration basin follows from that. With flow, waste character and dosing unchanged, the cause lies in clarifier operation such as sludge removal, rather than in the inflow or the chemicals.
questions.hint: A rising blanket means solids are not settling out.

questions.learningObjective: Choose well siting that reduces the risk of intrusion
questions.stem: Clinic note 102: a coastal clinic advises on well siting after saline intrusion has affected a village. Which practice reduces the risk?

options.text: Site the well below the saltwater interface, since deeper water is always fresher.
options.misconception: advises drilling into the saline zone

options.text: Site the well closer to the coast, so pumping draws fresher water upward.
options.misconception: advises siting a well where the lens is thinnest

options.text: Site the well in the shallowest aquifer available, since shallow aquifers resist intrusion.
options.misconception: believes shallow aquifers resist saltwater intrusion

options.text: Site the well farther inland, where the freshwater lens is thickest.

questions.explanation: The freshwater lens is thickest inland, and the saline interface lies offshore of it, so a well placed inland has the largest margin before the interface is reached. Shallow aquifers and positions below the interface are more exposed, not less.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Plan monitoring that can detect land subsidence
questions.stem: Clinic note 104: a district must build a monitoring programme that can detect land subsidence before it damages infrastructure. Explain what such a programme should include.

answer.exemplar: The programme needs a network of stable benchmarks on structures founded deep enough to be outside the compacting zone, because a benchmark on shallow fill or on the ground surface itself would record the local compaction of the soil rather than the movement of the land surface. Each benchmark should be surveyed at the same interval, ideally every year, and the readings processed together to give both a rate of subsidence for each point and a map of the sinking areas. Rates should then be compared with abstraction records for the same area and periods, so that the pattern of compaction can be related to pumping, and the network should be extended with additional deep benchmarks where the rates are highest.

questions.explanation: Benchmarks must be founded below the compacting zone, or they will track local soil compaction rather than the surface. Repeated surveys give a rate and a map, and comparison with abstraction records tests the pumping explanation.
questions.hint: Anchor the benchmarks deep and survey them regularly.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a soil survey record for contamination risk

stimulus.body: A soil survey for a new clinic site reports that the topsoil horizon is 10 centimetres thick over a subsoil of 45 centimetres, that the topsoil has a sandy loam texture with 1 percent organic matter, and that a shallow borehole found a perched water table at 30 centimetres sitting above a low permeability clay layer.

questions.stem: Clinic note 106: a survey for a clinic site reports a 10 centimetre topsoil of sandy loam with 1 percent organic matter over subsoil, and a perched water table at 30 centimetres above a low permeability clay. What does this imply?

options.text: The clay layer will protect the site, because low permeability stops all downward movement.
options.misconception: treats low permeability as complete protection rather than a barrier above a saturated zone

options.text: Contaminants would leach readily from the thin topsoil and collect above the clay layer.
The site is unsuitable, because a perched water table proves the soil is permanently saturated.
options.misconception: reads a perched water table as proof of permanent saturation

options.text: The thin topsoil will hold all nutrients, because sandy loam with organic matter retains strongly.
options.misconception: claims sandy loam retains nutrients strongly

A clay layer is therefore a barrier that traps contaminants above it rather than a protection.

It comes only from vehicles and industrial plants, so other sources are not regulated.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how overuse converts a renewable resource into a depleted one
questions.stem: Clinic note 110: a health officer is asked why a fishery or a well that was once regarded as inexhaustible can become a failing resource. Explain how that change happens.

answer.exemplar: A renewable resource can be used indefinitely only while the rate of withdrawal stays at or below the rate of replenishment. When a fishery is fished harder than the stock can reproduce, or a well is pumped faster than recharge can replace, the standing stock begins to fall, and the abundance that supported the use declines with it. The feedback that follows makes the decline worse: smaller populations produce fewer young, so the replenishment rate falls further, and in a well a lower water table reduces the yield of each unit of pumping. A resource in that state is still nominally renewable, but the stock has been reduced to a level that no longer supports the previous use.

questions.explanation: Renewability depends on rates staying balanced, and over-use drives the stock down until replenishment itself weakens. The resource then fails even though the natural process could in principle have continued.
questions.hint: Over-use lowers the stock and then the recovery rate.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the mass of coagulant needed for a given treatment flow
questions.stem: A treatment plant processes 3 million litres of water each day and doses coagulant at 25 milligrams per litre. How many kilograms of coagulant are required each day?
questions.explanation: The daily mass is 25 milligrams per litre times 3000000 litres, which is 75000000 milligrams, and that is 75 kilograms. The calculation needs the flow converted to litres, since the dose is given per litre.
questions.hint: Multiply the dose by the litres treated each day.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a monitoring record of chloride and interface movement

stimulus.body: A coastal bulletin reports chloride in a monitoring well rising from 180 to 410 milligrams per litre between two surveys four months apart, and the modelled position of the saline interface in that direction of flow moving inland by 60 metres over the same period. Pumping records show the well ran continuously through the period.

questions.stem: Clinic note 112: a bulletin reports chloride rising from 180 to 410 milligrams per litre in four months with the modelled interface advancing 60 metres inland, and the well running continuously. What does the bulletin show?

options.text: The well is safe, because the interface has moved inland and away from the pumping direction.
options.misconception: mislocates the direction of interface movement relative to the well

options.text: The rising chloride is a laboratory error, since the well is inside the freshwater lens.
options.misconception: assumes a position for the interface that the record contradicts

options.text: The chloride rise proves a new contamination source has entered the aquifer.
options.misconception: invents a new source where intrusion already explains the pattern

options.text: The well is drawing saline water as the interface approaches, so pumping should be reduced or relocated.

questions.explanation: A chloride rise of that size over four months, alongside an advancing interface and continuous pumping, is the expected signature of a well drawing saline water. It is a hydrological consequence of the pumping pattern rather than a new contamination source, and it needs a change in operations.
questions.hint: Rising chloride with a moving interface means intrusion.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Predict the effect of reducing pumping on subsidence
questions.stem: Clinic note 114: a coastal district reduces pumping after subsidence has damaged a road. Which statement describes what will happen to the land surface?

options.text: Subsidence reverses completely within a year of reduced pumping.
options.misconception: promises full and rapid recovery of compacted ground

options.text: Subsidence slows and partly reverses as pore pressure recovers, but some loss is permanent.
Nothing changes, because compaction of the aquifer is permanent by definition.
options.misconception: treats compaction as irreversible under all conditions

options.text: The land rises above its former level, because less water means less weight.
options.misconception: invents uplift above the original ground level

questions.explanation: Reducing pumping allows pore pressure to recover, which reverses the elastic part of the subsidence, while the compaction of fine sediments cannot be undone. The surface therefore rises slightly but stays permanently below its earlier level.
questions.hint: Elastic rebound yes, compaction no.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Plan a combined strategy for point and nonpoint pollution
questions.stem: Clinic note 116: a health board must set out a combined strategy for the point and nonpoint sources affecting one watercourse. Describe how the two should be handled and how success would be judged.

answer.exemplar: The point sources should be dealt with first and most precisely, because each outfall can be permitted, metered and upgraded, and a single plant may account for a large share of the load. The diffuse sources need a different instrument: nutrient management plans, cover crops over the winter, constructed wetlands at the edge of the watercourse, and limits on how close to the water manure may be spread, applied across the catchment rather than to one landowner. Success should be judged on the mass load delivered to the watercourse rather than on the concentration at a single station, which requires flow gauging, and on a network of monitoring sites sampled across seasons so that the diffuse contribution can be separated from the permitted discharges.

questions.explanation: Each source type needs its own instrument, and judging success on load rather than concentration requires flow data and sampling across seasons. Treating them as one problem with one instrument would leave part of the load unmanaged.
questions.hint: Different instruments, and judge the load not the concentration.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of a load contributed by a nonpoint source
questions.stem: A stream receives 500 kilograms per day of a pollutant from point sources and 1500 kilograms per day from nonpoint sources across the catchment. What percentage of the total load is nonpoint?
questions.explanation: The total load is 500 plus 1500, which is 2000 kilograms per day, and the nonpoint share is 1500 divided by 2000, which is 0.75 or 75 percent. Knowing the split tells the board how much of the problem can be addressed by permitting alone.
questions.hint: Divide the nonpoint load by the combined load.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Assess a soil profile description for contaminant vulnerability

stimulus.body: A soil pit for a proposed well site shows a dark topsoil horizon 15 centimetres thick, a red brown subsoil horizon with 30 percent clay extending to 2 metres, and pale grey sand below. A sample of the topsoil gives a cation exchange capacity three times that of the sand below, and the subsoil shows no signs of seasonal mottling.

questions.stem: Clinic note 118: a soil pit shows a 15 centimetre topsoil, a red brown subsoil of 30 percent clay to 2 metres, and pale sand below, with the topsoil holding three times the exchange capacity of the sand. What does this profile imply for a proposed well?

options.text: The absence of mottling shows the subsoil is permanently waterlogged and poorly aerated.
options.misconception: reads the absence of mottling as evidence of waterlogging

options.text: The sandy layer below means the site will be highly vulnerable, since the clay layer will be bypassed.
options.misconception: assumes groundwater bypasses the clay layer entirely

options.text: The clay-rich subsoil gives good protection, while the thin topsoil offers little capacity to hold contaminants.
The high exchange capacity of the topsoil means all contaminants will be retained there.
options.misconception: assumes high exchange capacity removes every contaminant

questions.explanation: The clay-rich subsoil provides a substantial barrier to downward movement, and the absence of mottling shows it is not waterlogged, so it retains its filtering capacity. The thin topsoil, however, has little capacity to hold contaminants before they are carried downward, which is why surface management at the site still matters.
questions.hint: The clay layer filters, but the topsoil is thin.
